chapter.name: Sequences and Series
chapter.blurb: This chapter treats a sequence as an ordered list of terms a(n), generated by a formula or a recurrence relation, and the series obtained by adding those terms, written with sigma notation. It then studies the geometric progression: its common ratio, general term a r^(n - 1) and the sum of its first n terms. It closes with the geometric mean of two positive numbers, inserting numbers to form a G.P., and the relationship A.M. >= G.M.

scope_in.item: Identify the terms of a sequence, use the notation a(n) for the nth (general) term, and say whether a sequence is finite or infinite
Find stated terms of a sequence from a formula for a(n), including formulas with fractions and alternating signs, and decide whether a given number is a term
Regard a sequence as a function whose domain is the set of natural numbers or a subset of it, and know that a sequence may be given by a verbal rule (primes) without a formula
Generate the terms of a sequence from a recurrence relation with given starting terms, including the Fibonacci sequence
Write the series associated with a sequence, distinguish a series from its sum, classify it as finite or infinite, and read or write sigma notation for a finite series
Recognise a geometric progression from the constant ratio of consecutive non-zero terms and find its common ratio
Use the general term a r^(n - 1) of a G.P. to find a term, the position of a given term, or the first term and common ratio from two given terms
Follow the derivation of the sum to n terms of a G.P. and use S(n) = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) for r not 1 and S(n) = na for r = 1
Find the sum of the first n terms of a G.P., the number of terms needed for a given sum, and a or r from given sums; evaluate a sigma sum that splits into a constant part and a G.P.
Find the geometric mean sqrt(ab) of two positive numbers and recognise a, G, b as a G.P.
Insert a given number of terms between two positive numbers so that the resulting sequence is a G.P., using b = a r^(n + 1)
State and justify A >= G for two positive numbers using A - G = (sqrt(a) - sqrt(b))^2 / 2, including when equality holds
Find two positive numbers (or a quadratic equation with those roots) from their arithmetic mean and geometric mean using (a - b)^2 = (a + b)^2 - 4ab

concepts.name: Sequences: terms, general term, finite and infinite sequences
concepts.description: A sequence as an ordered list (a function on the natural numbers), its terms a(n), the general term, finite and infinite sequences, and finding terms from a formula for a(n).
concepts.idea: A sequence is a list with an identified first, second, third, ... member. The nth term a(n) is the number in the nth position; a sequence need not have a formula, only a rule.
concepts.rule: Put n = 1, 2, 3, ... into the formula for a(n) to get the terms. A sequence with a fixed number of terms is finite; otherwise it is infinite.

Two sequences are defined by a(n) = n^2 - n and b(n) = 2n - 2. Find every position n at which the two sequences have the same term, and explain what this shows about identifying a sequence from its first few terms.
questions.a: a(n) = b(n) gives n^2 - n = 2n - 2, so n^2 - 3n + 2 = 0, (n - 1)(n - 2) = 0, n = 1 or n = 2. Indeed a(1) = b(1) = 0 and a(2) = b(2) = 2. But a(3) = 6 while b(3) = 4, so the sequences are different. Two different sequences can agree in their first few terms, so a few terms alone do not fix a sequence; the rule for a(n) is needed.
s: Sets n^2 - n = 2n - 2 and reduces to n^2 - 3n + 2 = 0
Solves to get n = 1 and n = 2 (common terms 0 and 2)

concepts.name: Recurrence relations, series and sigma notation
concepts.description: Sequences generated by a recurrence relation (such as the Fibonacci sequence), the series associated with a sequence, the sum of a finite series and the sigma notation.
concepts.idea: A recurrence relation builds each term from earlier ones, starting from given first terms. Adding the terms of a sequence with + signs gives the associated series.
concepts.rule: The series a(1) + a(2) + ... + a(n) is written Sigma (k = 1 to n) a(k). 'Series' is the indicated sum; 'sum of the series' is the number obtained.

concepts.name: Geometric progression: common ratio and general term
concepts.description: Recognising a G.P. from its constant ratio, finding the common ratio, and using the general term a r^(n - 1) to find terms, positions and unknown a or r.
concepts.idea: In a G.P. every term after the first is the previous term multiplied by the same non-zero number r, the common ratio.
concepts.rule: a(k + 1)/a(k) = r for all k >= 1, and the nth term is a(n) = a r^(n - 1).
concepts.example: In a G.P. with a r^2 = 24 and a r^5 = 192, dividing gives r^3 = 8, r = 2, a = 6, so the 10th term is 6 * 2^9 = 3072.

concepts.name: Sum to n terms of a G.P.
concepts.description: The formula for the sum of the first n terms of a G.P., its derivation, the case r = 1, and its use to find sums, the number of terms and unknown a or r.
concepts.idea: Multiplying S(n) by r shifts every term one place; subtracting cancels all but the first and last pieces, leaving (1 - r) S(n) = a - a r^n.
concepts.rule: S(n) = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1) for r not equal to 1; S(n) = na for r = 1.

s: States that the sum formula uses r^n (r^(n - 1) is for the nth term), so Sana is right
Confirms S(4) = 80, e.g. by adding 2 + 6 + 18 + 54

concepts.name: Geometric mean and inserting numbers in G.P.
concepts.description: The geometric mean sqrt(ab) of two positive numbers and the insertion of n numbers between two positive numbers so that the resulting sequence is a G.P.
concepts.idea: The G.M. of a and b is the middle term G that makes a, G, b a G.P. More generally, any number of terms can be inserted between a and b to form a G.P.
concepts.rule: G = sqrt(ab). If n numbers are inserted between a and b, then b = a r^(n + 1), so r = (b/a)^(1/(n + 1)) and the kth inserted number is a r^k.
concepts.example: Three numbers between 1 and 256: r^4 = 256, r = 4, giving 4, 16, 64.

concepts.name: Relationship between A.M. and G.M.
concepts.description: The arithmetic mean (a + b)/2 and geometric mean sqrt(ab) of two positive numbers, the inequality A >= G, and finding two numbers from their A.M. and G.M.
concepts.idea: For two positive numbers the arithmetic mean is never smaller than the geometric mean, because their difference is half a perfect square.
concepts.rule: A - G = (sqrt(a) - sqrt(b))^2 / 2 >= 0, so A >= G. Given A and G: a + b = 2A, ab = G^2 and (a - b)^2 = (a + b)^2 - 4ab.
concepts.example: A = 10, G = 8: a + b = 20, ab = 64, (a - b)^2 = 400 - 256 = 144, so the numbers are 4 and 16.

questions.a: Given a + b = 6 sqrt(ab). Divide by b and put t = sqrt(a/b) > 1: t^2 + 1 = 6t, so t^2 - 6t + 1 = 0 and t = 3 + 2 sqrt(2) (taking the root greater than 1). Then a/b = t^2 = 17 + 12 sqrt(2). Since (3 + 2 sqrt(2))(3 - 2 sqrt(2)) = 9 - 8 = 1, we have (3 + 2 sqrt(2))/(3 - 2 sqrt(2)) = (3 + 2 sqrt(2))^2 = 17 + 12 sqrt(2). Hence a : b = (3 + 2 sqrt(2)) : (3 - 2 sqrt(2)).

Any one earns full marks.)
